**Small GPU tasks can spend more time waiting for dispatch than doing arithmetic.** Suppose a workload has 100 tiny operations, each with an illustrative 3 microseconds of launch overhead and 2 microseconds of useful work. Repeated CPU dispatch can become a substantial part of the timeline. CUDA Graph replay submits a previously captured operation sequence with much less repeated setup. The numbers here illustrate the mechanism; they are not a hardware benchmark. [1](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/)

Think of recording a production schedule and replaying it with new materials in the same input buffers. The operations and their dependencies are already established. This does not make a large matrix multiply mathematically cheaper; it removes orchestration work around the GPU operations.

**Replay needs stable execution assumptions.** The captured path uses fixed buffer addresses and a known operation structure. Applications often use persistent buffers and shape buckets, copying new input into those buffers before replay. Different shapes or branches may require another captured variant or an ordinary execution path; supported graph updates are implementation-dependent.

Include capture and warmup cost when judging short-lived jobs. For serving, also account for memory reserved by graph variants and padding wasted by buckets. Inspect the CPU/GPU timeline first: replay is compelling when dispatch gaps matter, but it may barely change a workload already dominated by large compute-bound kernels.

**Technical details and references.**

CUDA Graphs record a GPU operation sequence and replay it with much less CPU launch overhead. This is useful when many small kernels finish so quickly that dispatch gaps dominate small-batch decode latency. [1](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/)

Captured execution needs stable operation structure and memory-address assumptions; supported updates and multiple graph variants can accommodate some changes, so “all dynamic behavior is impossible” is too strong. Allocate and warm up appropriately, avoid unsupported capture-time operations, and use fixed buffers or shape buckets when required.

Graph replay does not reduce the mathematical workload or guarantee a speedup for large compute-bound kernels. Account for capture cost, graph memory, padding/bucketing waste, and fallback paths. Verify numerical parity and measure CPU/GPU timelines to confirm launch overhead was actually the bottleneck.
